questions.stem: According to collision theory, which conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
options: Any amount of energy, as long as the particles collide head-on
Energy at least equal to the activation energy, and the correct orientation
Energy at least equal to the enthalpy change, and the correct orientation
Energy at least equal to the activation energy, at any orientation
questions.explanation: Particles must collide with enough energy to break the necessary bonds (the activation energy) and be lined up so the reacting parts meet. Collisions that fail either condition simply bounce apart.

questions.stem: What is the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The energy difference between the reactants and the products
The energy needed to heat the reactants to their boiling point
The minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur
The total energy released when the products of the reaction form
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the energy barrier between reactants and products on an energy profile. The energy difference between reactants and products is the enthalpy change, ΔH.

questions.stem: Which change increases the rate at which zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid?
options: Using a larger flask for the same mixture
Using zinc powder instead of a single lump
Using more dilute hydrochloric acid
Cooling the acid in an ice bath
questions.explanation: Powdered zinc exposes far more surface to the acid, so collisions happen more often. Diluting or cooling the acid slows the reaction, and the size of the flask does not change how often the particles collide.

questions.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of an acid increase its rate of reaction with magnesium?
options: The acid particles line up in the correct orientation more often
More acid particles per unit volume make collisions more frequent
Each collision between acid particles and magnesium has more energy
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra particles
questions.explanation: A higher concentration packs more reacting particles into the same volume, so they collide with the magnesium more often per second. The energy of each collision and the activation energy are unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the main reason a small rise in temperature greatly increases reaction rate?
options: A much larger fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy
The activation energy of the reaction falls as the temperature rises
The particles grow larger, so they are more likely to collide
The reaction changes from endothermic to exothermic when heated
questions.explanation: At a higher temperature particles move faster, so they collide slightly more often, but the bigger effect is that many more collisions have energy equal to or above the activation energy. The activation energy itself does not change.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate powder reacts faster with hydrochloric acid than the same mass of large chips. Why?
options: Powder has a lower activation energy than chips of the same compound
Powder particles have more kinetic energy than particles in large chips
Powder contains more moles of calcium carbonate than the same mass of chips
More particles are exposed, so collisions with the acid are more frequent
questions.explanation: Only particles at the surface of a solid can collide with the acid. Grinding increases the surface area, so more collisions happen each second. The amount in moles is the same for equal masses.

questions.stem: Adding a catalyst speeds up a reaction. How does it achieve this?
options: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
It gives the reactant particles more kinetic energy
It increases the enthalpy change of the reaction
It is used up, which releases energy to the reactants
questions.explanation: A catalyst offers an alternative route with a lower energy barrier, so a larger fraction of collisions are successful at the same temperature. It is not used up and does not change ΔH.

questions.stem: In a gas mixture, many collisions have more than enough energy to react, yet no reaction occurs. What is the most likely reason?
options: The activation energy rises during each collision with too much energy
The particles collide in an orientation that keeps the reacting atoms apart
The particles have too much energy, so they bounce apart instead of reacting
The collisions are too frequent, so the particles have no time to react
questions.explanation: Energy alone is not enough: the parts of the molecules that react must meet. Collisions at the wrong angle are unsuccessful whatever their energy.

questions.stem: Marble chips react with excess hydrochloric acid, and the volume of CO₂ is plotted against time. Why does the gradient of the curve decrease over time?
options: Reactants are used up, so successful collisions become less frequent
The activation energy rises as more carbon dioxide is produced
The carbon dioxide produced acts as a catalyst for the reverse reaction
The temperature rises, which slows down the movement of the particles
questions.explanation: As the reaction proceeds, the marble is used up and the acid becomes less concentrated, so there are fewer successful collisions each second. The curve becomes flat when the limiting reactant, the marble, is gone.

questions.stem: Two experiments use the same mass of calcium carbonate with the same volume of excess acid: one with chips and one with powder. How do the graphs of CO₂ volume against time compare?
options: The powder curve is steeper at first and reaches a larger final volume
Both curves have the same initial gradient, but the powder gives more gas
The chips curve is steeper at first, but both reach the same final volume
The powder curve is steeper at first, but both reach the same final volume
questions.explanation: A larger surface area increases the rate, giving a steeper initial gradient. The amount of calcium carbonate is the same, and it is the limiting reactant, so the final volume of gas is the same.

questions.stem: In the disappearing cross experiment, sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid to form a sulfur precipitate. What is measured to compare rates?
options: The mass of sulfur collected by filtering after a set time
The rise in temperature of the mixture until the cross disappears
The time for the precipitate to hide a cross under the flask
The volume of sulfur dioxide gas collected in a gas syringe
questions.explanation: The cloudiness from the sulfur precipitate builds up until the cross can no longer be seen. A shorter time means a faster reaction, so the rate is taken as proportional to 1/time.

questions.stem: Both heating and adding a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction. How do their effects differ?
options: Heating increases the enthalpy change; a catalyst makes the reaction more exothermic
Heating changes the products formed; a catalyst only changes how quickly they form
Heating gives more particles enough energy to react; a catalyst lowers the energy needed
Heating lowers the energy needed to react; a catalyst gives more particles enough energy
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature leaves the activation energy unchanged but shifts more particles above it. A catalyst leaves the particles' energies unchanged but provides a pathway with a lower activation energy.

questions.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
options: It absorbs heat from the surroundings, and ΔH is positive
It releases heat to the surroundings, and ΔH is negative
It absorbs heat from the surroundings, and ΔH is negative
It releases heat to the surroundings, and ΔH is positive
questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction the products have less chemical potential energy than the reactants, and the difference is released as heat, so the surroundings warm up and ΔH is negative.

questions.stem: Which process is endothermic?
options: Respiration of glucose in cells
Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water
Burning methane in a gas stove
Neutralising hydrochloric acid with NaOH
questions.explanation: Dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs heat, which is why it is used in instant cold packs. Combustion, neutralisation and respiration all release heat.

questions.stem: Solid barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride are mixed in a flask, and the flask becomes very cold. What does this show?
options: The reaction has a very high activation energy, so it absorbs cold
The reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive
The reaction releases heat into the surroundings, so ΔH is positive
The reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, so ΔH is negative
questions.explanation: The flask cools because the reaction takes in heat from it and the surroundings. Energy is absorbed, so the products have more chemical potential energy than the reactants and ΔH is positive.

questions.stem: Explained in terms of bond breaking and bond forming, what makes a reaction exothermic?
options: More energy is released forming new bonds than is absorbed breaking old ones
More energy is absorbed breaking old bonds than is released forming new ones
Energy is released both when old bonds break and when new bonds form
No bonds are broken, so all of the energy of bond formation is released
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and forming bonds always releases it. If the bonds formed are stronger overall than those broken, the net energy is released as heat.

questions.stem: Where does the heat released by an exothermic reaction come from?
options: Kinetic energy taken from the walls of the reaction vessel
Chemical potential energy, as products store less than reactants
Energy created when the new bonds in the products are formed
Energy released as the bonds in the reactants are broken
questions.explanation: By the law of conservation of energy, energy is not created. The products have lower chemical potential energy than the reactants, and this difference appears as heat. Breaking bonds absorbs energy rather than releasing it.

questions.stem: Use these bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242, H-Cl 431. What is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl?
options: −1109 kJ mol⁻¹
−184 kJ mol⁻¹
+184 kJ mol⁻¹
+247 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released forming bonds = (436 + 242) − (2 × 431) = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting that two H-Cl bonds form gives +247.

questions.stem: Use these bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): C-H 414, O=O 498, C=O 803, O-H 463. What is ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O?
options: −420 kJ mol⁻¹
−806 kJ mol⁻¹
+806 kJ mol⁻¹
−3458 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: Bonds broken: 4 C-H + 2 O=O = 1656 + 996 = 2652 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 C=O + 4 O-H = 1606 + 1852 = 3458 kJ. ΔH = 2652 − 3458 = −806 kJ mol⁻¹. Subtracting the other way round gives +806.

questions.stem: On an energy profile diagram, what does the peak of the curve represent?
options: The point at which the reaction gives out the most heat
The reactants, before any collisions between them occur
The transition state, where bonds are breaking and forming
The products, once all of the new bonds in them have formed
questions.explanation: The peak is the highest-energy arrangement along the reaction pathway, the transition state. The height from the reactants to the peak is the activation energy.

questions.stem: Which describes the energy profile diagram of an endothermic reaction?
options: The products and reactants are at the same energy, so ΔH is zero
The products are higher in energy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive
The products are lower in energy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive
The products are higher in energy than the peak, so ΔH is negative
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction energy is absorbed, so the products end up with more chemical potential energy than the reactants. The peak is still above both.

questions.stem: On an energy profile, the reactants are at 50 kJ mol⁻¹, the peak at 180 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 20 kJ mol⁻¹. What are the activation energy and ΔH?
options: Ea = 160 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 130 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 180 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −30 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea = 130 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: Ea is measured from the reactants to the peak: 180 − 50 = 130 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = products − reactants = 20 − 50 = −30 kJ mol⁻¹, so the reaction is exothermic. 160 is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

questions.stem: On an energy profile, the reactants are at 50 kJ mol⁻¹, the peak at 180 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 20 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
options: 30 kJ mol⁻¹
180 kJ mol⁻¹
160 kJ mol⁻¹
130 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction starts from the products at 20 kJ mol⁻¹ and must climb to the same peak at 180 kJ mol⁻¹, so its activation energy is 160 kJ mol⁻¹. 130 kJ mol⁻¹ is the forward activation energy.

questions.stem: A catalyst is added to an endothermic reaction. How does its energy profile change?
options: The peak is higher, so the reaction absorbs more energy from the surroundings
The reactants rise to a higher energy, closer to the top of the peak
The peak is lower, but the reactant and product energies are unchanged
The products fall below the reactants, so the reaction becomes exothermic
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both endothermic and exothermic reactions by offering a different pathway. The reactants and products are the same substances, so ΔH does not change.

questions.stem: What does the specific heat capacity of a substance measure?
options: The highest temperature it can reach before it boils
The energy released when 1 mol of it burns completely
The energy needed to raise 1 g of it by 1 K
The energy needed to melt 1 g of it at its melting point
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Water's value, 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, is high, so water needs a lot of energy to warm up.

questions.stem: 1000 J of heat is added to 100 g samples of copper (c = 0.385), aluminium (c = 0.90) and water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). Which has the largest temperature rise?
options: Water, because it has the highest specific heat capacity
Aluminium, because it is the least dense of the three
All three equally, because their masses are equal
Copper, because it has the lowest specific heat capacity
questions.explanation: ΔT = q/(mc), so the substance with the smallest c heats up most: copper rises about 26 °C, aluminium 11 °C and water only 2.4 °C.

questions.stem: Use c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 250 g of water by 20.0 °C?
questions.explanation: q = mcΔT = 250 × 4.18 × 20.0 = 20 900 J = 20.9 kJ. A temperature change of 20.0 °C is the same as 20.0 K. Writing 20 900 with kJ units overstates the energy a thousandfold.

questions.stem: Use c(aluminium) = 0.90 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the temperature rise when 1000 J is added to 100 g of aluminium?
questions.explanation: ΔT = q/(mc) = 1000/(100 × 0.90) = 11 °C. Using water's specific heat capacity gives 2.4 °C, which is why metals warm up far faster than water.

questions.stem: 2440 J of heat raises the temperature of 100 g of liquid ethanol by 10.0 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of ethanol?
options: 24.4 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹
0.410 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹
244 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹
2.44 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹
questions.explanation: c = q/(mΔT) = 2440/(100 × 10.0) = 2.44 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Inverting the expression gives 0.410.

questions.stem: Use c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What mass of water can be heated from 20.0 °C to 100.0 °C by 33.4 kJ of energy?
questions.explanation: m = q/(cΔT) = 33 400/(4.18 × 80.0) = 99.9 g, or 100 g. Using 20.0 °C as the temperature change gives 400 g, and forgetting to convert kJ to J gives 0.100 g.

questions.stem: In a polystyrene-cup calorimeter, the temperature of the solution rises during a reaction. What is the sign of ΔH for the reaction?
options: Negative, because the reaction releases heat to the solution
Positive, because the solution gains heat from the reaction
Negative, because the reaction absorbs heat from the solution
Positive, because the temperature of the solution increases
questions.explanation: The heat gained by the water, q, comes from the reaction, so the reaction loses energy. That is why ΔH = −q/n: a positive q for the water means a negative ΔH for the reaction.

questions.stem: 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ NaOH, and the temperature rises by 6.7 °C. Take the solution as 100 g with c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is ΔH of neutralisation?
options: −2.80 kJ mol⁻¹
−56.0 kJ mol⁻¹
−28.0 kJ mol⁻¹
+56.0 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: q = 100 × 4.18 × 6.7 = 2800.6 J. n(H₂O formed) = 0.0500 mol. ΔH = −q/n = −2800.6/0.0500 = −56 000 J mol⁻¹ = −56.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Using only 50 g of solution gives −28.0.

questions.stem: 5.00 g of ammonium nitrate (M = 80.05 g mol⁻¹) dissolves in 50.0 g of water and the temperature falls by 7.7 °C. Assume the heat comes only from the 50.0 g of water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹). What is ΔH of solution?
options: −25.8 kJ mol⁻¹
+1.61 kJ mol⁻¹
+322 kJ mol⁻¹
+25.8 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: q = 50.0 × 4.18 × (−7.7) = −1609 J, and n = 5.00/80.05 = 0.0625 mol. ΔH = −q/n = +1609/0.0625 = +25 800 J mol⁻¹ = +25.8 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature fell, so the process is endothermic. 1.61 is q in kJ before dividing by n.

questions.stem: Burning 0.46 g of ethanol (M = 46.07 g mol⁻¹) in a spirit burner raises the temperature of 200 g of water by 10.0 °C. Use c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the experimental ΔH of combustion?
options: −8.36 kJ mol⁻¹
−837 kJ mol⁻¹
−18.2 kJ mol⁻¹
+837 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation: q = 200 × 4.18 × 10.0 = 8360 J, and n = 0.46/46.07 = 0.00998 mol. ΔH = −8360/0.00998 = −837 000 J mol⁻¹ = −837 kJ mol⁻¹. Dividing by the mass instead of the amount gives −18.2 kJ g⁻¹.

questions.stem: A spirit-burner experiment gives ΔH of combustion of ethanol as −837 kJ mol⁻¹, but the data book value is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the main reason?
options: The specific heat capacity of water was too high to use in the calculation
Heat was lost to the air and the can, so less heat reached the water
The water absorbed extra heat from the room, so the rise was too large
More ethanol burnt than was weighed, so too much heat was produced
questions.explanation: Much of the heat from an open flame warms the surrounding air and the metal can rather than the water, and some ethanol may burn incompletely. Less heat reaching the water makes the experimental value less negative than the true value.

questions.stem: The experimental ΔH of combustion of ethanol is −837 kJ mol⁻¹, and the accepted value is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |experimental − accepted|/accepted × 100 = 530/1367 × 100 = 38.8%. Dividing by the experimental value instead gives 63.3%.

questions.stem: Which change would most improve the accuracy of a simple calorimetry experiment for a reaction in solution?
options: Using an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid
Using a glass beaker so the reaction can be seen
Stirring less often to stop heat being produced
Using a larger volume of water than of solution
questions.explanation: Heat lost to the surroundings is the largest error in simple calorimetry. Polystyrene is a good insulator and a lid reduces losses from the surface, so more of the heat is measured as a temperature change.

questions.stem: What is an economic advantage of using a catalyst in an industrial process?
options: The final yield of product at equilibrium is greatly increased
Products form quickly at a lower temperature, which reduces energy costs
The catalyst is used up and can then be sold as a valuable by-product
The enthalpy change is made larger, so more heat can be sold to users
questions.explanation: A catalyst lets a reaction run at a useful rate at lower temperature and pressure, saving fuel and equipment costs, and it is not used up, so it can be reused. It does not change ΔH or the equilibrium yield.
